package_info.package_manager: bundled with freeware (not a traditional package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: Fireball is considered malicious because it hijacks web browsers by modifying browser settings, changing DNS configurations, and enabling the execution of arbitrary code or the download of additional malware. This allows attackers to monetize user traffic, inject advertisements, and further compromise infected systems, often without user consent or awareness.

execution_context.trigger: at system startup or browser launch
execution_context.file_location: browser configuration files (e.g., prefs.js for Firefox, registry entries for Chrome/IE), browser extension directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Modifies browser default homepage and search engine settings to attacker-controlled values by writing to browser configuration files or registry keys.
malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (JavaScript for extensions, registry scripts, or compiled binaries depending on infection vector)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At system startup or browser launch, the code writes attacker-controlled URLs to browser configuration files or registry keys, redirecting the homepage and search engine, resulting in user traffic and search queries being sent to malicious servers for monetization.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unauthorized modification of browser settings to redirect user traffic is a hallmark of browser hijackers and adware, especially when performed without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not alter browser homepage or search engine settings without explicit user permission and clear notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise management tools or group policies may set browser defaults for compliance, but these changes are typically transparent to users and managed by administrators.
key_indicators: Direct modification of browser configuration files or registry keys
Homepage and search engine set to non-standard, attacker-controlled URLs
No user prompt or consent for browser setting changes

execution_context.trigger: after initial infection or on specific browser events
execution_context.file_location: browser process memory (via injected code), downloaded payloads in temporary or system directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Executes arbitrary code or downloads and runs additional malware payloads from remote servers by injecting code into browser processes or launching downloaded executables.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After initial infection or on specific browser events, the code establishes outbound connections to attacker-controlled servers, downloads additional payloads, writes them to disk, and executes them, enabling further compromise or persistence on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The ability to download and execute code from untrusted remote servers is a critical security risk, enabling attackers to escalate privileges, install more malware, or exfiltrate data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal browser extensions or software should not execute arbitrary code or download and run untrusted binaries, especially without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download updates, but only from verified sources and with user consent, and typically use code signing to ensure authenticity.
key_indicators: Outbound connections to untrusted or known malicious domains
Download and execution of unsigned or unexpected binaries
Code injection into browser or system processes

execution_context.file_location: browser content scripts, system DNS configuration files (e.g., /etc/resolv.conf on Unix, registry on Windows)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Manipulates browser content and DNS settings to redirect traffic or inject advertisements by altering DNS server addresses and injecting scripts into web pages.
malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (JavaScript for content scripts, system scripts, or compiled code for DNS changes)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During active browsing sessions, the code modifies DNS settings at the system or browser level and injects scripts into web pages, redirecting user traffic to attacker-controlled sites and displaying unauthorized advertisements, increasing monetization and exposing users to further threats.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Changing DNS settings and injecting ads into web content without user consent is a classic sign of adware and browser hijackers, often used to redirect traffic and increase ad revenue.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not alter DNS configurations or inject advertisements into browser sessions without clear user consent and transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Parental control or security software may filter DNS or inject warnings, but these actions are disclosed to users and serve a protective purpose.
key_indicators: Unauthorized changes to system or browser DNS settings
Presence of injected scripts or ads in web pages not originating from visited sites
Redirection of web traffic to unexpected or non-standard domains

attack_chain.action: Malware is installed on the victim's machine via bundling with freeware, often without clear user awareness.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial execution and establishment of persistence mechanisms

attack_chain.action: On execution, the malware modifies browser settings to hijack the homepage and search engine, redirecting user traffic.
attack_chain.leads_to: User traffic and search queries are redirected to attacker-controlled servers for monetization

attack_chain.action: Malware manipulates browser content and DNS settings to inject advertisements or redirect traffic to malicious sites.
attack_chain.leads_to: Increased ad revenue for attackers and potential exposure of users to further threats

attack_chain.action: Malware executes arbitrary code or downloads and runs additional payloads from remote servers, further compromising the system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Installation of additional malware, persistence, and possible data exfiltration

behavioral_signatures: Unauthorized modification of browser homepage or search engine settings to non-standard URLs
Injection of advertisements or scripts into web pages not originating from visited domains
Unexpected changes to system or browser DNS configuration
Execution of code or download of binaries from untrusted remote servers
Creation or modification of browser extensions without user consent
file_indicators: Altered browser configuration files (e.g., prefs.js for Firefox, registry keys for Chrome/IE)
Presence of unknown or unsigned browser extensions or plugins
Unexpected scripts or binaries in browser or system directories (e.g., AppData, Program Files, browser extension folders)
Modified system DNS configuration files (e.g., /etc/resolv.conf, Windows registry keys: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters)
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known adware or malware command-and-control domains
Unusual DNS queries or changes to DNS server settings (e.g., DNS servers not matching ISP or organization defaults)
HTTP/HTTPS requests to download additional payloads from untrusted or previously unseen domains
Frequent connections to domains associated with ad injection or browser hijacking
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unauthorized changes to browser settings and DNS configurations by auditing browser and system configuration files. Detect the installation or modification of browser extensions without user consent. Analyze network traffic for connections to known malicious or adware domains, unexpected DNS server changes, and downloads of executable files from untrusted sources. Use endpoint protection to detect code injection, browser hijacking behaviors, and the execution of unsigned binaries. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify and block Fireball infections.
